text:
F.K. c. H.K.

2016 QCCS 6065

JM2232

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N°:

500-17-080069-134

DATE:

December 7, 2016

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF THE HONOURABLE
PAUL MAYER, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

F.K.

PLAINTIFF

v.

H.K.

DEFENDANT

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGEMENT

______________________________________________________________________

1.         INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This case concerns two brothers who have become
irreconcilable enemies.  It is an account of alleged sexual abuse and mental
illness that has split a family apart.

[
2
]

In short, F.K. reveals that, some 30 years ago,
his older brother H.K., sexually assaulted him over a period of nearly a
decade.  He seeks $999,999 in damages.

[
3
]

H.K. says that he is both angry and sad about
the abusive procedures and the false allegations he submits are without merit.
Further, he contends that the recourse is prescribed given that the last
assault is said to have occurred in 1984.  He asks for moral and punitive
damages and requests that F.K. be declared a litigant subject to
authorization.  He reserves the right to claim the legal fees and disbursements
incurred to defend himself.

2.         LEGAL ISSUES

[
4
]

The Court proposes to examine the following
issues:

a)

has F.K. met his burden of proof to establish
that H.K. committed the alleged sexual assaults?

b)

in the event that he has, is the claim
prescribed?

c)

if not, what are the damages caused by H.K.?

d)

in the event that F.K.’s action is dismissed, is
H.K. entitled to:

i)

moral damages? and

ii)

punitive damages?

e)

should F.K. be declared a litigant subject to
authorization?

3.         HAS
F.K. MET HIS BURDEN OF PROOF TO ESTABLISH THAT H.K. COMMITTED THE ALLEGED SEXUAL
ASSAULTS?

3.1       The
Context

3.1.1    The
Parties

A.         F.K.

[
5
]

F.K. was born in 1967.  He is a 49 year-old
bachelor.  He has a B.A. in English literature from the
Université de Montréal
and a
Master
of Library and Information Studies
from McGill University.  Since 1998, he
has worked on and off for various libraries and governmental departments.

B.        H.K.

[
6
]

H.K. is five years older than F.K., his only
sibling.  He is a married father of three children and a business man who
specializes in the rental of lakefront cottage properties.
[1]

3.1.2    Their
childhood

[
7
]

The parties agree on one thing.  They both grew
up in an exceptionally chaotic environment, that is, a “
house full of
turmoil
”.  The parents were tormented souls in constant conflict.  Fights
could go on for hours.  There was a lot of screaming and verbal abuse, as the
parents argued with each other for all sorts of reasons.  The police had to
intervene on a number of occasions.  Sometimes, they were called by the neighbours.
At other times, they were sent for by the parties themselves.

[
8
]

The father had a singularly difficult
childhood.  He could be gregarious and talkative, but he also had a dark side.
He was an angry man who could not control his temper.  He was bellicose and
would often quarrel.  As he was often unemployed, the family was not wealthy.
He passed away in 2011.

[
9
]

The mother had no role models to show her how to
be a parent since she had been orphaned early in life.

[
10
]

H.K. was better able to cope with this turmoil.
He broke free more easily, as he had many friends.

[
11
]

H.K. acknowledges that F.K. had a terrible
childhood.  He felt trapped, as he had few friends.  He was very odd, and he
interacted strangely with other kids.  He would often lock himself in his
room.  He became obsessed by the
Star Trek
TV show.

[
12
]

When F.K. was between the ages of 3 and 8, the
family lived in a three-bedroom upper-duplex apartment on A Avenue, in City A.
Each boy had their own room.

[
13
]

Then, between the ages of 8 to 16, he shared a bedroom
with H.K. in a 4 ½ room apartment on B Street, in City A.

3.1.3    The
alleged first assault

[
14
]

F.K. says that the first assault occurred on A
Avenue, when he was 8 years old.  He recalls that H.K. was in the bathroom with
his friend Andy. They called him in and asked him to lie down on the bath mat
and to take his pants down.  It is here that H.K. would have sexually abused
him for the first time.

[
15
]

Emerging from the bathroom after the incident,
he says that he went directly to the kitchen where his mother was busy.  He
remembers telling her about it.  She dismissed him.  Apparently, she did not
want to investigate or take the matter seriously.

3.1.4    The
following assaults

[
16
]

Subsequently, the alleged sexual assaults were
carried out by H.K. on average once a week, for the next decade.

[
17
]

F.K. recalls specifically that the second
assault was violent.  He says that H.W. climbed on his back and that he
penetrated him.  He held him with his arm around his neck and he threatened
him:  “
Don’t tell mommy or daddy, or I’ll kill you
”.
[2]
He says he took the threat seriously.  He was also worried that if
he told either his father or his mother, they would have killed him.

[
18
]

He reveals that the assaults became a regular
habit.

[
19
]

It is only thanks to his gaining adolescent
consciousness and to the sex education courses in high school that he began to
understand that the relationship with his brother was abnormal.
[3]

[
20
]

He reveals that he started to resist the
assaults as he grew older.  He says that the last assault occurred in June 1984
when he was 17 years old.  He observes that it was particularly violent and
painful.
[4]

3.1.5    The
alleged sexual assaults by his mother

[
21
]

F.K. alleges that not only did his mother make
no effort to defend him from the sexual assaults of H.K., but she was also
sexually aggressive with him.

[
22
]

F.K. remarks that his mother was sexually
frustrated because his father was impotent. She began to show a sexual interest
in him in the early 1980s.  He remembers that she would sexually harass him.
She would come on to him, hug him and kiss him in an unnatural and overtly
sexual way.

[
23
]

Once she lunged at him as she wanted to grab him
sexually.  He tried to repel her.  Pushing her backwards, she fell.  He says
that as a result of his refusal of her sexual advances, she directed H.K. to
beat him up.
[5]

[
24
]

He remembers that H.K. warned him not to refuse
the sexual advances of his mother.  He came to his room, broke the lock and
battered him.  He fought back and called the police, but they refused to
intervene.

3.1.6    The
prejudice

[
25
]

F.K. describes the prejudice he suffered because
of the assaults.  He says that:

a)

he is silent and introverted;

b)

his relations with women have been adversely
affected.  He has never been married, nor has he had a steady girlfriend;

c)

although he had been a good student until grade
9, he was expelled from high school in grade 11, having missed too many
classes;  he did not complete
CEGEP
;
[6]

d)

he had a severe depression in 1982;

e)

the scientific career that he dreamed of,
particularly in the areas of the cosmos and space exploration, was destroyed by
H.K.;

f)

he suffers from severe mental issues and needs
psychological help; and

g)

he is not able to keep a job for very long.

[
26
]

He insists that the problems he suffers from,
confirm or give support to the story of sexual assaults which he asserts.

3.1.7    Dr.
Charles Levin

[
27
]

F.K.’s version of events is believed by Dr.
Charles Levin.  He is a psychologist who treated F.K. for a short period of time
in 1990 following a car accident.  He remembers that F.K. was an emotionally
disturbed individual who had a difficult childhood.  He reveals that F.K. told
him about the sexual assaults towards the end of his treatment.

[
28
]

He is convinced that F.K. is telling the truth
because it explains his deep psychological problems.

3.1.8    Denials
by H.K., his mother and his father

[
29
]

H.K. thoroughly denies all of the “
highly
offensive
” allegations put forward by F.K.  He insists that the alleged
events never happened and that F.K. is suffering from mental incapacities and
delusional thoughts.  He does not understand why he is making all of this up.
He believes that he may be jealous of him and his spouse, S., who F.K.
unsuccessfully tried to seduce some 25 years ago.

[
30
]

In a detailed affidavit dated June 4, 2014, his mother
also denies all of F.K.’s allegations.  She states that F.K. did not tell her
that he was the subject of any type of abuse by H.K., nor did she ever see any
signs that could possibly indicate that H.K. assaulted F.K.

[
31
]

Rather, she observes that F.K. showed signs of
mental instability and social awkwardness during his childhood.  He spent a
significant amount of time following the TV show
Star Trek
hyper
obsessively.  Because of this, he began to lose touch with reality.  As such,
he could not bear to go to high school.  Following a car accident in 1989, his
behavior became worse.

[
32
]

She reveals that F.K. lived with her and her
husband on and off until he was 34 years old.

[
33
]

In summary, she claims to be left speechless by
the suit that F.K. has initiated.

[
34
]

Before passing away in 2011, his father denied
in a sworn statement the allegations made by F.K. against H.K.
[7]

3.2       Analysis
and decision

[
35
]

How does one discern the truth or falsity of
this story?  Where does the truth lie?

[
36
]

To a great extent, the outcome of this case
depends on the Court’s appreciation of F.K.’s credibility.

[
37
]

One of the most difficult aspects of a judge’s
work is the evaluation of a witness’s credibility, given that it is at best an
imprecise science.  Such an assessment can only be done by a critical
examination of all of the evidence submitted.

[
38
]

The real test of the truth in a story rests in
its harmony with the preponderance of probabilities, that is, would a practical
and informed person readily recognize it as reasonable in the circumstances?
Does the story make logical sense, or is it so farfetched as to require the
Court to abandon all notion of common sense?

[
39
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court
determines that F.K.’s Re-Amended Motion to Institute Proceedings and his
testimonial evidence raise concerns both as to veracity and accuracy. There are
serious troubles with his ability to relate what actually occurred and to
accurately recount the events in question.  In short, the Court does not
believe he is either credible or reliable.

[
40
]

F.K.’s version of the facts is, from all
appearances fictional and completely bizarre.  This is manifest upon a simple
reading of his Re-Amended Motion and his examination before plea.  It is even
more evident when listening to his testimony. Many elements of his claim are not
in harmony with the preponderance of probabilities.

3.2.1    An
obsession with sexual matters

[
41
]

To begin with, it is obvious that F.K. has an obsession
or preoccupation with matters of a sexual nature that is not rational or
sensible.  His mind appears to be contaminated by the topic.

[
42
]

Among other things, F.K. asserts that in the
early 1980s, H.K. began an incestuous relationship with his cousin S. when she
was 11 and he was 21.
[8]
H.K. denies this completely. Firstly, he says that S. lived in
Winnipeg until 1999 and that it was not until that year that they became
romantically involved.  Secondly, he points out that S. is not his biological
cousin, as she had been adopted by his aunt and uncle.  H.K. has been living
with her since the year 2000.  They have two children, born in 2001 and 2010.

[
43
]

F.K. contends that when H.K. was a teenager, he
spent numerous afternoons and evenings at the next door neighbours’ house,
where alcohol was served.  He suspects that drugs were consumed and that H.K.
was used as “
a sexual play thing
”.
[9]

H.K. denies this.  Rather, he states that the neighbour taught him how to build
model airplanes, a hobby he continues to be passionate about to this day.

[
44
]

F.K. mentions that in 1978 (when he was 11 years
old), he was sent to a Camp, in City B, Quebec. He relates that it was “
his
bad luck
” that he ended up bunking with eight boys, six of them being
practicing homosexuals “
who engaged in sex every night
”.
[10]
He pleaded with his parents to rescue him, but they refused.  He,
thus, learned “
a lasting lesson about the unreliability and uselessness of
his parents
”.
[11]

[
45
]

In her sworn affidavit, his mother denies that
she ever received any letters from him pleading to be rescued from the said summer
camp.  She writes that if she had ever received anything that hinted at the
sexual acts that F.K. is alleging, she would certainly have removed him from
that environment.  H.K. further points out that it is unlikely that young 11
year-old boys would participate in such activities.  He also recalls that at
this camp, a counsellor slept in the cabin with the campers.

[
46
]

F.K. tries to dismiss his mother’s affidavit.
He says that she did not write it herself.  He declares that it is “
a bunch
of junk, lies and inventions
”!  He believes that H.K. “
forced her to sign
it
:
it’s a form of elder abuse
”.

[
47
]

F.K. declares that, as early as 1975, H.K. was
having homosexual sex parties with his close male friends.
[12]
In his examination before plea and during his testimony at trial,
he recalled in considerable detail the numerous male friends involved. F.K. also
says that H.K. was very popular with girls and that he had many girlfriends.
[13]

[
48
]

H.K. denies the allegations made by F.K. of
homosexual parties.  He comments that the thought of it rather disgusts him,
and he insists that he is heterosexual.  One of the alleged friends, David,
signed a sworn affidavit denying the allegations.

[
49
]

Finally, the Court notes that F.K. has made a
number of other sexual abuse accusations over the years that have not held up.

[
50
]

In 1992, F.K. filed a complaint of sexual
harassment with the
Commission des droits de la personne
against the
owner of a food store where he worked for a period of about three weeks.  The
complaint was dismissed.

[
51
]

Then, in April 1993, he filed a criminal
complaint with the Montreal police against Mrs. D., who had been his girlfriend
from May to September 1991.  They had sexual intimacy some two dozen times
during their romantic relationship.  Some 19 months after she broke up with
him, he accused her of having kidnapped, sequestered and sexually assaulted
him.  The Crown decided not to press charges.

[
52
]

In his Re-Amended Motion to Institute
Proceedings, he relates that when he made his complaint to the police against
Mrs. D. in 1993, he was “
insulted, vexed and threatened
” by them and
that this made him “
distrustful of police officers
”.
[14]

[
53
]

In his examination before plea of February 10,
2014, he was asked why the said police officers had threatened and insulted
him?  He replied:

“
They asked me if I took my Lithium today.  So, they insinuated
that I take Lithium, and they told me that there’s a special ward in the
basement of Louis H … Louis-Hippolyte Hospital … a special ward in the basement
where they have freaks of nature who are kept there, like people born with only
one (1) eye, people born with a tail, other kinds of freaks, and that that’s
where I belong.
”
[15]

[integral text]

[
54
]

Questioned why the police officers of Station 25
would say such things to him, he said it was because they were incompetent and
because they hate everybody:

[…]

A multi-part answer.  I can assume it’s for the same reason that the
Montreal Police administration shut down Station 25 concerned in that article,
and never reopened it.  It could be for the same reason that the Just For
Laughs gags … T.V. show is allowed to use the police cars numbered Station 25,
because Station 25 is a big joke that nobody takes seriously as a police
station.

I can also assume it’s because the officers there were incompetent,
because they hate everybody, and I can also assume it’s for the same reasons
that they have had bad relations with everybody in that neighbourhood, of the
Concordia ghetto, where they were ill placed and ill suited to serve …
[16]

[integral text]

[
55
]

He made the same allegations of sexual assault
and filed another criminal complaint with the Montreal police against Mrs. D.
in 2002.  This grievance was also dismissed.

[
56
]

Obviously, the Court considers that there is
something wrong with this story.  F.K. was not living with Mrs. D. at the
time.  If he had been raped by her once, why would he go back and be the victim
of more assaults over a further four-month period?  These allegations of sexual
assault against Mrs. D. do not make logical sense.

3.2.2    F.K.’s
distrust and fear of police officers

[
57
]

As illustrated hereinabove, F.K.’s version of
his relationship with police officers appears to be so totally fictional and
outlandish, that one can only conclude that his version of those events is not
realistic or sensible.  There is more, however.

[
58
]

One observes that in his Re-Amended Motion, F.K.
declares that:

a)

in 1982 (when he was 13 years old), the City A
police were called to the family home whereupon they threatened to murder him
by “
running over him with a truck
”;
[17]

b)

in 1983, the police, called to the family home
again, threatened to beat him “
with a heavy police flashlight
;
[18]

c)

in 1984, he called the police, following a
severe beating by his brother, but they refused to help him;
[19]

d)

in 2002, when he made a criminal complaint with
the City A police against his brother for the alleged assaults, a police
officer threatened to help his brother “
obtain an injunction against him to
induce him to commit suicide by drowning
”.
[20]

[
59
]

At the Hearing, he asserts that during the 2002
investigation of his criminal complaint against his brother, a police officer
suspected him of being the
Zodiac Killer
(a serial killer who operated
in Northern California in the late 1960s and 1970s, whose identity remains
unknown) and an associate of the Sicilian American crime boss, Sam Giancana,
who died in 1975 (when F.K. was 7 years old).

[
60
]

In 2004, he wrote a seven-page letter to the
Commissaire
à la déontologie policière
criticizing the two police officers of the City
A Police Department with respect to their investigation.

[
61
]

The gist of his grievance was that they “
gave
false and misleading information to the Crown based on their own personal
failure to investigate the case properly
”.  He wrote that the officers were
particularly hostile against him and that they did “
everything within and
without their power to side with the abusers or organize a smear campaign
against him
”.
[21]

[
62
]

This complaint was also dismissed.  All of these
allegations of police misconduct in respect to him do not appear to be rational
or fair-minded.

3.2.3    F.K.’s
numerous complaints

[
63
]

The evidence also shows that F.K. has filed an
inordinate amount of complaints against physicians, lawyers, co-workers, civil
servants and employers, who, he alleges, have wronged him.  Their enormous
volume and their tone and content illustrate that F.K. is unstable and that he
appears to have lost grip with reality.  The following are a number of examples
that demonstrate this.

3.2.3.1
SAAQ

[
64
]

In 1989, F.K. was hit by a car as he was
crossing a street.  In 1994, he sought a review of two decisions made in 1991
by the
Société de l’assurance automobile du Québec
(the “SAAQ”) to:

a)

cease payment of the income replacement
indemnity paid to him, effective November 2, 1989; and

b)

refuse to reimburse him the psychotherapy fees
of Dr. Charles Levin, beyond June 18, 1990.

[
65
]

At first, he was represented by Mtre. Guy
Saint-Aubin in this matter.  In a three page letter, dated April 18, 1994, he
relates that he fired Mtre. Aubin because, among other things, he had made
“
inaccuracies
” in a letter dated in March 1994.  In that same letter,
F.K. complained about the services of Mr. Guy Michaud of the
SAAQ
.
He found him to be an “
extremely hostile and intimidating person
”. He
blamed him for having prevented him from respecting the 60-day time limit to
appeal the 1991
SAAQ
decisions.  He also alleged numerous procedural
errors and abuse of power by Mr. Michaud that made it impossible for him to get
a proper hearing.
[22]

[
66
]

In a 10-page sworn statement to the
SAAQ
,
dated June 10, 1994, in support of his appeal, F.K. complained that he had many
difficulties finding competent health care and that he had to change doctors
many times because of this.  He also criticized the “
error, oversight,
incompetence, malfeasance and negligence
” committed by the
SAAQ
’s
employees, subcontractors and doctors.
[23]

[
67
]

Among others, he found fault with Dr. Kim-Anh Do
who committed procedural errors that compromised his rights and which “
ruined

[his]
mental health since that time
”.
[24]

[
68
]

Further, he observed that the medical exam
performed by Dr. Copti was “
flawed, incomplete, inaccurate and dishonest
”.
According to F.K., he was “
extremely insecure, hostile and untrusting
”.
He says that he was bullied into submission by him and that he made “
particularly
vicious fabrications
”.  He considered that “
he is not concerned with the
wellbeing of his patients
”.  F.K. concluded his statement by stating that
Dr. Copti was an extremely hostile, dishonest and vicious person.  He
considered that his medical report “
should be declared null and void
”.
[25]

[
69
]

His appeal was dismissed.

[
70
]

H.K. also relates that, following the 1989 car
accident, F.K. made a complaint against his neurologist, Dr. Robert Lefrançois.

3.2.3.2
Brooklyn Public Library

[
71
]

In the year 2000, F.K. moved to New York City to
work with the Brooklyn Public Library.  The evidence shows that he logged many
complaints of discrimination and harassment against his employer and his
co-workers during his two-year period of employment.

[
72
]

On March 26, 2002, the Assistant Human Resource
Director wrote him a memorandum to respond to five written complaints he had
made in a three-month span between November 26, 2001 and February 6, 2002.  He
stated that the library had seriously considered and thoroughly investigated
each complaint but that they had not been able to substantiate any of them, and
that no evidence of discrimination or harassment was found.

[
73
]

It is noted that in December 2001 he was placed
in sick-leave violation for excessive absences.  The memorandum indicates that
his conduct “
in repeatedly raising complaints that have already been
investigated by the library constitute bad faith
”.  This would no longer be
tolerated.  It announces that the following grievances that had been raised and
addressed would no longer be entertained:

•

Religious discrimination; arising out of your
complaints while working at Ulmer Park.

•

National origin Canadian; arising out of your
complaints while working at Ulmer Park.

•

Gender discrimination; you alleged while
working at Ulmer Park.

•

Civil status (single male); complaint you
raised while at Ulmer Park.

•

Sexual orientation based upon a patrons
complaint against you; complaint filed while working at Ulmer Park.

•

Physical assault you alleged occurred after
you ate an employees lunch when you worked at the Ulmer Park branch.

•

Blackmail you alleged occurred over
documentation (customer complaints) about your performance when you worked at
Ulmer Park.

•

Political views of the staff differed with
you in general and particularly on the holocaust and antisemitism created a
hostile work environment while at the Ulmer Park branch.

•

Smoking complaint you filed while working at
Ulmer Park, and your request for excused time which was denied.

•

Conspiracy to prevent professional
advancement while you were at Ulmer Park.

•

Harassment you alleged occurred by Mr.
Kenneth Azic during employee orientation of 2/14/00.

•

Health benefits which you alleged were denied
during your orientation of 2/14/00.

•

Dental benefits which you alleged were denied
during your orientation of 2/14/00.
[26]

[integral text]

[
74
]

The memorandum concludes that upon finishing the
drafting of same, the Human Resources Officer received two new complaints
logged by F.K. in which he alleged being discriminated against, based on
national or ethnic origin.  He also found fault about a gas leak that had
occurred and that no action was taken.  Finally, he claimed that he had a
disability for which he was requesting an accommodation.

[
75
]

During the Hearing, F.K. tried to undermine the
reliability of the author of the memorandum by saying that he had tried to
murder one of his friends.

[
76
]

It is no great surprise to learn that he left
that employment some three months later in June 2002.

3.2.3.3
Complaint against Dr. Judith Vogel

[
77
]

F.K. states that he told Dr. Judith Vogel,
his psychiatrist, of the sexual assaults in the summer of 1986 during either
the final or penultimate session with her “
before
[he]
outgrew her
”.
He further says that she failed to report the assaults.

[
78
]

Some 28 years later, in January 2014, F.K. filed
a complaint against her with the
Collège des médecins du Québec
.  He states
that he saw her every week from September 1981 to July 1986.  He writes that
she “
rudely insulted
” him with respect to his obsession with the
Star
Trek
television program.  He accuses her of having inflicted and invented
false psychological problems on him.  He says that in the nearly five years of
seeing him, she “
simply never did anything for me
”.  According to him,
the entire experience was a “
waste of his valuable time
”.
[27]

[
79
]

He mentions that she experimented with
non-medical techniques without his consent.  He accuses her of having done
nothing and taken no action when he reported having suicidal thoughts.  Nor did
she report the sexual assaults by his brother.  He protests that Dr. Vogel
should have reported the crime to the police and that she was negligent not to
do so.  He states further that when he made the criminal complaint to the
police in 2002 against his brother, she was uncooperative and she would not
help in providing information.

[
80
]

Finally, he writes that when he contacted the
hospital to ask for proof that the crimes had been reported to the police “
as
is the law
”, he was “
rudely insulted
” and “
ridiculed
” by the
hospital “
many times
”, including by their lawyer.
[28]

[
81
]

This complaint was also dismissed.

3.2.3.4
Complaints against Court workers

[
82

4.         IS
THE CLAIM PRESCRIBED?

[

]

Given the conclusion reached hereinabove, it is

however, the fact that both parties spent considerable time and energy on this
topic, the Court will address it.

4.1       The
law

[
143
]

Article 2925
of the
Civil Code of Quebec

stipulates that an action in damages, such as this one, is prescribed by three
years.
[60]

[
144
]

Article 2904 C.C.Q. provides an exception to
this general rule.
[61]
Prescription does not run against persons if it is impossible for
them to act by themselves or to be represented by others.

[
145
]

The impossibility to act by victims of sexual
assaults has been examined on a number of occasions in jurisprudence.

[
146
]

The leading case on this issue is the Supreme
Court of Canada decision in
M.(K.)
v.
M.(H.)
[62]
.  Although it is a common law case, it is
nevertheless pertinent with respect to certain basic principles.  It sets out
that the
prerequisite for a plaintiff to act is that
he:

[…]
have a substantial awareness of the harm and its likely cause
before the limitation period begins to toll.  It is at the moment when the
incest victim
discovers
the connection between the harm she has suffered and her childhood
history that her cause of action crystallizes.

[
147
]

The case of
Christensen

v.
Archevêque catholique romain de Québec
[63]
examines the starting point of prescription in a similar fashion:

[134]  Le délai de prescription ne
peut pas commencer à courir avant le jour où, pour la première fois, le
détenteur du droit à exercer pouvait effectivement prendre une action en
justice, c’est-à-dire à compter de ce jour où, pour la première fois, il
connaissait, ou pouvait raisonnablement connaître, les trois éléments
nécessaires à l’exercice de son recours (la faute, le préjudice et le lien de
causalité entre la faute et le préjudice).  Ce n’est, en définitive, qu’à
compter de ce moment que les conditions juridiques du droit de poursuite se
trouvent enfin réunies et que la cause d’action se cristallise.

[
148
]

At times, the
impossibility to act can be caused by fear. Such unease can lead to a lack of
introspection and to an inability to speak about the secret surrounding the
sexual assault.  It is a common occurrence that a victim will not reveal it to
his family and friends because there is a concern about what they will think.

[
149
]

In the Supreme
Court of Canada case of
Gauthier
v.
Bromont
[64]
, the Court writes the following with respect to the criteria to be
examined when evaluating the fear factor:

To be a cause of impossibility to act, the fear must be of an
objectively serious harm, must exist throughout the period when it was
impossible to act and must subjectively be determinative of this impossibility
to act, that is, subjectively such that it is psychologically, if not
physically, impossible for the victim to take legal action.

[
150
]

This case teaches us the need to be flexible in
evaluating the circumstances surrounding the impossibility to act in cases of
sexual assaults.  One needs to examine the context of each particular case and
to adopt a relatively subjective analysis centered on the victim.

[
151
]

The 2011 Court of Appeal decision of
P.L.

v.
J.L.
[65]
, reminds us that it is necessary to interpret the issue of
prescription liberally when examining the inability to act in similar
situations:

(46) les règles de la prescription, dans les affaires d’inceste,
doivent être appliquées avec souplesse et à la lumière des circonstances. À mon
avis, il faut analyser l’impossibilité d’agir, dans les cas d’inceste, en étant
conscient des difficultés pour les victimes de faire le lien entre les
préjudices qu’elles ont subis, qui peuvent parfois être latents, et les
agressions.

[
152
]

The application of this liberal analysis is not,
however, without limit.  One must keep in mind the overriding tenet that
provides that the suspension of prescription is an exception to the general rule.
Article 4 C.C.Q. reminds us that every person is presumed to be fully able to
exercise his civil rights.
[66]

[
153
]

Hence, the Court of Appeal, in the case of
Catudal

v.
Borduas
[67]
evokes the principle that the burden of
proof is on a plaintiff to establish (on the balance of probabilities) that he
had the absolute psychological impossibility to take a judicial claim in a
timely manner:

(71) Cette décision [
Catudal c. Borduas
] illustre le lourd fardeau
dont doit s’acquitter celui qui allègue avoir été dans l’impossibilité
psychologique d’agir. De plus, une chose demeure certaine, peu importe la
source de l’impossibilité, elle doit avoir privé la victime de son libre
arbitre, de sorte que celle-ci n’a pas volontairement renoncé à l’exercice de
son droit.

[
154
]

Having, thus, set out the applicable legal
criteria to the case at hand, it is appropriate to examine the position of each

7.2       The
law

[
218
]

Article 1621 C.C.Q. specifies that punitive
damages can be awarded when such award is provided for by law.
[79]

[
219
]

The threshold requirement of this article is set
forth in Article 51 and following of the
Code of Civil Procedure
which stipulate
that when a Court declares that there has been an abuse of procedure, it may,
among other things, award punitive damages and order a party to pay the
professional fees and disbursements incurred by the other party.

[
220
]

The Supreme Court case of
Whiten
v.
Pilot
Insurance Company
[80]

sets out the underlying principles to
be applied in such circumstances:

[94]  To this end, not only should the pleadings of punitive damages
be more rigorous in the future than in the past (see para. 87 above), but
it would be helpful if the trial judge’s charge to the jury included words to
convey an understanding of the following points, even at the risk of some
repetition for emphasis.

(1) Punitive damages are very much the exception rather than the
rule,

(2) imposed only if there has been high-handed, malicious,
arbitrary or highly reprehensible misconduct that departs to a marked degree
from ordinary standards of decent behaviour.

(3) Where they are awarded, punitive damages should be assessed in
an amount reasonably proportionate to such factors as the harm caused, the
degree of the misconduct, the relative vulnerability of the plaintiff and any
advantage or profit gained by the defendant,

(4) having regard to any other fines or penalties suffered by the
defendant for the misconduct in question.

(5) Punitive damages are generally given only where the misconduct
would otherwise be unpunished or where other penalties are or are likely to be
inadequate to achieve the objectives of retribution, deterrence and
denunciation.

(6) Their purpose is not to compensate the plaintiff, but

(7) to give a defendant his or her just desert (retribution), to
deter the defendant and others from similar misconduct in the future
(deterrence), and to mark the community’s collective condemnation (denunciation)
of what has happened.

(8) Punitive damages are awarded only where compensatory
damages, which to some extent are punitive, are insufficient to accomplish
these objectives, and

(9) they are given in an amount that is no greater than necessary to
rationally accomplish their purpose.

(10) While normally the state would be the recipient of any fine or
penalty for misconduct, the plaintiff will keep punitive damages as a
“windfall” in addition to compensatory damages.

(11) Judges and juries in our system have usually found that
moderate awards of punitive damages, which inevitably carry a stigma in the
broader community, are generally sufficient.

[95]  These particular expressions are not, of course,
obligatory.  What is essential in a particular case will be a function of
its particular circumstances, the need to emphasize the nature, scope and
exceptional nature of the remedy, and fairness to both sides.

[
221
]

In the Court of Appeal decision of
Cinar

v.
Robinson
[81]
, it is noted that the abovementioned Supreme Court of Canada case
has a limited application in Quebec, given the codification of the criteria set
out in Article 1621 C.C.Q.  The Court does,
nevertheless, state that punitive damages are justified “
dans le cas d’une
conduite malveillante et répréhensible qui déroge aux normes usuelles de la
bonne conduite. Ils sont accordés dans le cas où les actes répréhensibles
resteraient impunis ou lorsque les autres sanctions ne permettraient pas de
réaliser les objectifs de châtiment, de dissuasion et de dénonciation.
”

[
222
]

The Court must, therefore, decide if F.K.’s

and reprehensible.

were old photographs of Mtre. Ayda Abedi, his attorney who conducted F.K.’s examination
before plea of February 2014.

[
248
]

He concludes that this anonymous mail comes from
F.K.  It is his way of showing that he can scare people.  He wants to hurt him
and his spouse.  According to him, the present situation is fun for F.K.  He
likes to provoke people.

[
249
]

The Court considers that there is some truth to
this as F.K. was observed laughing several times during his testimony.  At
other times, he joked with respect to extremely serious and sensitive matters.
He appeared to be having fun.  The only time he displayed any emotion, is when
he described his problems graduating from high school.

[
250
]

For example, asked why he was claiming the sum
of $999,999, he replied in jest that if his brother gives him a cheque of $1M,
he has a loonie in his pocket for him.  H.K. does not share his brother’s sense
of humour.  He states that this award would bankrupt him.  It is no laughing
matter for H.K. and his family.

[
251
]

This created a distinct impression that F.K. was
using the Court system to harm H.K., his spouse and his mother. This is what is
described in Article 51 C.P.C. as an attempt to defeat the ends of justice.
F.K. must realize that the law is not a heartless beast.  The legal system is a
public good.  It is not (to use his expression) to be used as a tool deployed
to “
rattle someone’s cage
”.

[
252
]

The Court concludes that H.K., his spouse, his
mother, his children and the judicial system need to be protected from F.K.’s vexatious
obsession.  They must be safeguarded against his quest for revenge and his toxic
hatred that perverts his perception of the world.  He is dangerous due to his
unreason.

[
253
]

Accordingly, F.K. will be declared a litigant
subject to authorization and he will be prohibited from instituting legal
proceedings against them without authorization of the Chief Justice.
